# Entering a New Region: A Sustainable Apparel Playbook

*Two expansions wearing one coat — and the arithmetic that decides which market you can actually afford*

---

## 1. Unbundle the Request Before Choosing a Map

"Access new customer segments **and** manufacturing opportunities" is two expansions with different geographies, different capital profiles, different owners and different failure modes. Fusing them is the most expensive error available here.

| | **Track D — Demand** | **Track S — Supply** |
|---|---|---|
| **Objective** | Revenue growth outside a saturating Western European base | Capacity, cost, capability, fibre access, resilience |
| **Optimal geography** | Where willingness-to-pay for premium sustainable apparel is high and retail is curated | Where certified fibre, skilled making and audit-ready factories exist |
| **Capital profile** | Working capital + brand investment; slow payback | Deposits, tooling, QA headcount; faster payback |
| **Owner** | Commercial / brand | Product & sourcing / COO |
| **Time to signal** | 12–24 months | 3–6 months (first sampling round) |
| **Failure mode** | Burning cash on customer acquisition in a market that never adopts | Quality collapse, compliance exposure, single-source dependency |

These almost never point at the same country. **Run them as parallel tracks with separate budgets and separate gates.** The only legitimate coupling is technical — free-trade-agreement rules of origin (§3), which make the sourcing decision determine the tariff you pay in the sales market.

> **Standing rule:** you may co-locate the two tracks only if the demand case survives on its own merits with the sourcing benefit set to zero. "We're already there" is not a market-entry thesis; it is how brands end up selling €95 shirts in a market whose premium apparel ceiling is €40.

---

## 2. Select the Market from Revealed Demand, Not Desk Research

Before commissioning a market study, mine what you already own. A mid-sized brand with a Western European footprint has more evidence than it thinks.

**The revealed-demand audit (2–3 weeks, near-zero cost):**

| Signal | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Unserved web traffic and cart abandons by country | Where demand exists that your checkout currently refuses |
| Existing international orders — volume, AOV, return rate, repeat rate | Return rate by market is the single best early predictor of fit and expectation mismatch |
| Inbound wholesale enquiries from foreign retailers | Unpaid buyer signal; also tells you which retailers already believe in the aesthetic |
| Organic search demand for your category, in local language | Whether a category exists or must be created — the latter is 5× the budget |
| Where your closest European comparables have succeeded *and* failed | Failures are more informative and are usually undocumented; ask their ex-employees |

Then screen candidates on a small, weighted set. Resist twenty-criterion scorecards — they always produce the answer the largest market wants.

| Screen | Threshold-style question | Kill signal |
|---|---|---|
| **Willingness to pay** | Can your current architecture clear at local premium price points after duty and returns? | Requires >25% price cut to be viable |
| **Category maturity** | Does "sustainable premium apparel" already exist as a shelf, or must you invent it? | You'd be educating the market alone |
| **Route to credibility** | Are there 20–40 specialty retailers who would carry you? | Only mass channels exist |
| **Tariff & regulatory access** | Duty rate, FTA origin eligibility, labelling and green-claims regime | Effective duty >20% on your origin |
| **Cost to serve** | Freight, 3PL, returns rate, payment mix | Return rates >35% with no local returns solution |
| **Operational complexity** | Language, entity, tax, data, IP enforcement | Trademark already squatted |
| **Climate & seasonality fit** | Does your assortment work, or is it 60% redundant? | Southern-hemisphere inversion with no capsule |

---

## 3. The Recommendation

**Primary demand market: North America, entered through a two-step — Canada as the operational beachhead, a US metro cluster as the actual prize.**

**Hedge, run in parallel at 20% of the cost: Japan (extending to South Korea) via a local distributor or agent.**

**Supply track, independent of both: dual-source across Türkiye/Portugal (nearshore, speed, EU origin) and India (GOTS-certified organic cotton depth, cost, scale) — with a small owned sourcing/QA presence, and no owned factory.**

**Why this shape:**

| Rationale | Detail |
|---|---|
| **North America is where scale is** | The largest concentration of consumers who will pay a premium for the category, in English, with a mature specialty-retail infrastructure and press ecosystem |
| **Canada de-risks the US** | CETA gives duty-free access for **EU-origin** garments; a smaller, more forgiving market to debug sizing, fit, messaging, returns and 3PL before spending US-scale acquisition money. Treat it as a live pilot, not a market |
| **The US has no tariff preference and a volatile one** | Apparel duties commonly 10–32% by fibre and construction, plus a shifting country-specific overlay. Model this line item explicitly and re-check quarterly; it is not a rounding error |
| **De minimis is gone** | Direct-from-Europe parcel shipping into the US no longer escapes duty and formal entry. The old cheap-test path is closed — **US entry now requires domestic inventory or fully-landed DDP pricing.** Plan for it |
| **Japan/Korea are the margin play** | EU–Japan EPA and EU–Korea FTA can deliver **0% duty on EU-origin apparel**; high willingness to pay for material quality and construction; distributor model means low fixed cost. But rules of origin generally require double transformation — **garments cut and sewn in India or Türkiye will not qualify.** This is the one place the two tracks genuinely interact |
| **India is a supply market now, a demand market in year 3+** | Premium price points and retail structure make it a poor first sales market for a mid-sized European brand; fibre depth and certified capacity make it an excellent second source |

**Decision rule if you must pick one:** if >55% of your units are EU-origin and your AOV is above €120, lead with Japan (margin, low burn, curated distribution). If your strength is volume, breadth and English-language brand storytelling, lead with North America. Do not lead with both at full spend.

---

## 4. Positioning: Lead With the Garment, Close With the Ethics

In your home markets, sustainability is part of your equity. In a market where your brand equity is zero, it behaves differently:

- **Sustainability is rarely a reason to try you. It is a reason to stay with you.** First purchase is won on aesthetic, fit, feel, price-to-quality and trust in delivery. Retention and advocacy are won on values.
- **Do not moralise into a new market.** European-style environmental framing reads as instruction rather than invitation in North America, and as noise in Japan, where provenance, craft, material specification and longevity are the more powerful vocabulary for the same facts.
- **Your compliance history is a competitive weapon.** Substantiation you already carry for EU green-claims rules lets you make specific, verifiable statements where local competitors can only make vague ones. Convert compliance burden into specificity: not "eco-friendly," but *"organic cotton, GOTS chain-of-custody, spun in X, sewn in Y, 82 wash cycles tested."*

**The positioning ladder — build it explicitly, in this order:**

1. **Object claim:** it looks right, fits right, lasts. (This carries the first sale.)
2. **Proof claim:** specific, traceable, third-party certified. (This carries the price.)
3. **Identity claim:** what owning it says about the wearer, in local, not European, terms. (This carries the second purchase and the referral.)

**Assortment must be localised, not translated:**

| Adaptation | Why |
|---|---|
| Sizing and fit blocks | US fit runs looser and larger; Japanese and Korean fit runs smaller with different proportions. Shipping European blocks unchanged is the single most common cause of 40% return rates |
| Climate-driven capsule | Humid summers, harsher winters, different layering logic. Expect 20–35% of the range to be dead weight |
| Category weighting | Lead with 8–12 hero SKUs that carry the proof story, not the full line |
| Colour and print | Test, don't assume |
| Care labelling and language | Legally mandated and different in every jurisdiction (see §8) |

---

## 5. The Arithmetic: Model Landed Contribution Before You Model Revenue

Most failed apparel entries were arithmetically doomed at launch and discovered it in month 14. Build this table with your own numbers before any channel decision. Illustrative only:

| Per unit, DTC | Home market | New market (US, non-EU origin) |
|---|---|---|
| Retail price | €89 incl. VAT | $99 excl. sales tax ≈ €91 |
| Net revenue | €73.6 | €91.0 |
| COGS | €22.0 | €22.0 |
| Duty (16.5% on customs value) | — | €4.3 |
| Inbound freight + 3PL + last mile | €6.0 | €9.0 |
| Returns provision (15% vs 30% rate) | €5.0 | €14.0 |
| Payments & fees | €1.5 | €2.7 |
| **Contribution before acquisition** | **€39.1** | **€39.0** |
| Blended CAC, established vs new brand | €12 | €45–60 |
| **First-order contribution** | **+€27** | **−€6 to −€21** |

**Three conclusions follow immediately, and they should shape everything downstream:**

1. **Paid-social DTC as the primary entry channel is insolvent for a mid-sized brand with no local awareness.** It only works if you are underwriting a 9–15 month repeat-purchase payback with cash you have already committed.
